Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — Starting October 19, GitLab.com rate limits will align with your subscription. Sign in to unlock higher limits. Premium/Ultimate changes arrive in January.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — GitLab.com hosts millions of projects for teams of every size that need a platform they can rely on. Demand is climbing quickly, and we expect platform load to grow several times over this year. Predictable limits are what keep GitLab.com fast for everyone on it, including the automation and agent workloads teams are building on the platform.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — To hold that as we scale, we're updating how rate limits work. Starting October 19, 2026, rate limits on GitLab.com will align with your subscription tier. Free accounts and unauthenticated requests happen first, on October 19. Premium and Ultimate move in January 2027.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — What is changing
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — What is changing — Limits align with your subscription. Free, Premium, and Ultimate subscription plans get their own limits, applied per user and per top-level group. Free takes effect October 19; Premium and Ultimate in January 2027.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — What is changing — Signing in gets you the full limit. An authenticated request is governed by your subscription plan below. A request that arrives with no credentials gets 60 requests per hour per IP address.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — What is changing — The per-plan limits are published in the rate limits documentation .
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — What happens on October 19
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — What happens on October 19 — There will be two preview windows for Free and unauthenticated traffic, on October 7 and October 14 from 15:00 to 19:00 UTC. Signed-in Premium and Ultimate requests are not affected, since those limits do not change until January. Unauthenticated requests are capped no matter where they come from, including automation running against a paid account without credentials. A preview window (engineers call these brownouts) is a short, planned window where we switch the new limits on and then switch them back off. Nothing else about the service changes while it runs. The point is to give you a real look at how your own workloads behave under the new limits, weeks before they apply for good.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — What happens on October 19 — On October 19 the new limits take effect.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — What happens on October 19 — We set these limits by looking at how GitLab.com is actually used. Almost all users are already inside the new limits and won't notice any change. We also looked at what similar platforms allow. The Free limit and the anonymous allowance match the industry norm, while Premium and Ultimate are more generous, at levels other platforms reserve for their enterprise tiers or don't publish at all.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — If you're close to a limit
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — If you're close to a limit — If you find that you are nearing a limit, authenticate your requests. It's usually a small change: Invoking a personal access token , an OAuth token, or the CI/CD job token all move a request off the anonymous 60 requests per hour and onto your plan's limits, which are much higher.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — If you're close to a limit — Next, look at how you're calling the API. Batching, caching, and pagination go a long way, and polling in a tight loop burns through your allowance fast. When you do cross a limit, you get an HTTP 429 back with a Retry-After header saying how long to wait, so a client that reads its own response headers mostly fixes itself. Backing off exponentially recovers faster than retrying immediately.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — If you're close to a limit — Upgrading to Premium or Ultimate increases the limits, too, per user and per top-level group.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — If you're close to a limit — If you need a higher limit on an ongoing basis, we are working on a way to purchase capacity above the standard plan limits, with details coming later this year. If that sounds like you, reach out to your account team or email limits@gitlab.com and tell us what you need.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — What changes and what doesn't
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — What changes and what doesn't — These limits are set so no single workload can slow the platform for everyone else. Ordinary signed-in work isn't the target, and, for almost all users, a normal day looks identical. Browsing the UI, working in your editor, pushing and pulling with git, and running CI/CD within your plan all carry on exactly as they do today. Some heavy automation and a small number of Free-tier workloads will reach the new ceilings.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — What changes and what doesn't — What doesn't change:
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — What changes and what doesn't — You can always reach and export your own data and repositories.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — What changes and what doesn't — GitLab Self-Managed and GitLab Dedicated limits stay with your operator. This is only a GitLab.com change.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — What changes and what doesn't — We'll notify you before we make additional changes.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — What changes and what doesn't — A reminder: Make sure to authenticate your requests to GitLab.com so your limits are higher.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — FAQ
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — FAQ — How do I know whether this affects me? Compare your busiest minute against the published limits for your plan . Most customers are not close. The quickest signal in the meantime is the RateLimit-Remaining header on your API responses, which tells you how much of your current window is left, and we are building a view in the product for release later this year that shows your usage against your plan's limits.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — FAQ — My project is public and busy. What are my options? Three things help. Ask the automation that calls your project to sign in, which moves it onto its own limits rather than the anonymous allowance. Make the project private if the traffic is not coming from the audience you built it for, which stops anonymous callers reaching it at all. Or upgrade to Premium or Ultimate for much higher limits.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — FAQ — What if I am a member of several top-level groups? Your user limit will be the highest subscription tier available to you. If you are a member of an Ultimate group, you will have access to the Ultimate limit.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — FAQ — What happens when I hit a limit? You get 429 Too Many Requests with RateLimit-* headers and a Retry-After . Wait the interval it gives you, then retry.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — FAQ — My integration genuinely can't authenticate. What now? Reach out to us at limits@gitlab.com . There are legitimate anonymous patterns, a public status badge being the obvious one. If you are concerned that an integration you own may be affected, contact us.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — FAQ — Does this apply to GitLab Self-Managed or GitLab Dedicated? No. This is a GitLab.com-only change.
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — Additional resources
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — Additional resources — Rate limits by plan
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — Additional resources — Authenticating your API requests
Rate limits on GitLab.com are changing — Additional resources — Questions, or you've encountered a case we haven't thought of? Contact your account team or email limits@gitlab.com .

stories.headline: GitLab Announces Changes to Platform Rate Limits Starting in October
stories.deck: GitLab updates rate limits on GitLab.com to align with subscription tiers, beginning with Free accounts and unauthenticated traffic.

claims.text: GitLab announced that rate limits on GitLab.com will align with user subscription tiers, with Free accounts and unauthenticated requests updating first on October 19, 2026.
According to GitLab, Premium and Ultimate subscription plans will follow in January 2027, applying distinct limits per user and per top-level group.

stories.whyItMatters: These changes apply exclusively to GitLab.com, leaving GitLab Self-Managed and GitLab Dedicated deployments unaffected by the shift. Each subscription plan receives distinct limits applied per user and per top-level group. Unauthenticated requests arriving without credentials are capped at sixty requests per hour per IP address.
stories.whatToDoOrWatch: Review your busiest minute against published plan limits and check the RateLimit-Remaining header on API responses. Authenticate integration requests to move off the anonymous hourly cap. Watch for upcoming preview windows on October 7 and October 14 to test how workloads behave.

Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages.
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams.
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks.
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.

Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.

Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.
Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

Bransys ELD — Recommended Practices — CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. stories.headline: Bransys ELD Hardcoded MQTT and FTP Credentials Expose Real-Time Data and Server Files
stories.deck: According to CISA, multiple vulnerabilities involving hardcoded credentials and cleartext transmission could allow external connection and data access under specific broker conditions.

claims.text: CISA reports that CVE-2026-86520 affects the Bransys ELD product, which ships with hardcoded MQTT credentials that grant read access to real-time data for active devices across connected carrier subsets.
Additionally, CISA notes that CVE-2026-77960 involves hardcoded FTP credentials shipped in the affected product, potentially allowing an attacker to connect to the server and read stored data.

stories.whyItMatters: The security advisory applies specifically to Bransys Android versions prior to 11.00.00 and Bransys iOS versions prior to 1.1.54. Organizations running these known affected versions must verify their installed software scope to determine if their mobile deployments require immediate attention.
stories.whatToDoOrWatch: Users should review their app store availability and update their systems as recommended by the vendor. Android users should ensure their devices run version 11.00.00 or newer, while iOS users should be on version 1.1.54 or newer.
